title: Let Your Students Run the Conference
author: David Basulto
summary: David Basulto argues that parent-teacher conferences work better when the student runs the meeting and the teacher coaches from the side. The usual format, in which the teacher narrates the gradebook while the learner is absent, leaves the person who did the learning out of the conversation. Student-led conferences have long been practiced, he says, and what stopped teachers was the prep work of reflection sheets, talking points and agendas. He offers a copy-and-paste prompt that has Claude draft a student reflection sheet, sentence starters and a ten-minute agenda card in about fifteen minutes. He pairs it with a firm privacy rule that no student names ever go into the AI, a one-period prep and rehearsal plan, and a conference-day script with the teacher's two closing minutes. The piece is an explicit classroom workflow for teachers, with the AI doing drafting only and the teacher editing the output.
points: Order the student-run meeting as work samples, reflection, plan, and grades last, so the numbers arrive with context.
A single fill-in-the-brackets Claude prompt produces a reflection sheet, sentence starters and an agenda card in roughly fifteen minutes.
The privacy rule is that the AI receives structure (categories, units, grade level) while students supply names and work on paper.
A one-period prep day with work-sample selection, quiet reflection and partner rehearsal turns the kit into a usable conference.
When parents ask for the teacher version, confirming the student's account and adding one observation keeps the format intact.
quotes: Teachers have run student-led conferences for decades. The research behind them is not new. What stopped most of us was the prep: reflection sheets, talking points, an agenda, all of it differentiated enough that every kid can actually run a meeting.
Your job in the room: open the meeting, add one or two observations the student can’t see about themselves, and back up the plan. That’s it.
Read the output before you print it. Cut anything that doesn’t sound like your classroom, and ask Claude to revise anything generic. You’re the teacher. Claude is the copy machine that drafts.
The students add their own names, their own work samples, and their own reflections, on paper, in your classroom. The personal data never touches the tool.
This is the line I hold with every AI workflow I share: the AI gets the structure, the students supply themselves.
The rule I give them: at least one thing you’re proud of, at least one thing that was a fight. Nobody shows only their best work. The struggle piece is where the real conversation happens.
Then let them run it. Resist the urge to rescue. A kid fumbling toward “I didn’t turn in the lab write-ups and that’s why my grade dropped” is worth more than you saying it smoothly.
Say: “Everything she told you matches what I see. Here’s the one thing I’d add.” Then add it. You’ve validated the student, answered the parent, and kept the format intact.
